# Horner syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Neurosurgery > Horner syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/Ui0bIf)

---

## Summary

Horner syndrome (HS) is a neurological disorder characterized by a symptom triad of <u>miosis</u> (an abnormally small <u>pupil</u>), partial <u>ptosis</u> (drooping of the upper <u>eyelid</u>), and facial <u>anhidrosis</u> (absence of sweating). This condition results from lesions that interrupt the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>sympathetic</u> nervous supply to the head, <u>eye</u>, and neck. Most cases of HS are <u>idiopathic</u>, but conditions such as <u>brainstem</u> <u>stroke</u>, <u>carotid dissection</u>, and <u>neoplasm</u> are occasionally identified as the cause of HS. Because of the wide array of possible causes, diagnosis of the underlying disorder frequently poses a challenge and requires a systematic approach. Once the lesion has been identified, treatment should be tailored to the specific cause.

---

## Pathophysiology

| Overview |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Anatomical trajectory | Typical lesion |
| Central | <br>* <u>Hypothalamus</u> (first-order oculosympathetic neuron)  → <u>brainstem</u>, cervical, and thoracic spinal cord → ciliospinal center (C8–T2)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Brainstem</u> <u>stroke</u> (e.g., <u>Wallenberg syndrome</u>)<br><br>* Cervical <u>spinal cord injury</u> (e.g., <u>Brown-Séquard syndrome</u>, <u>syringomyelia</u>)<br><br>* <u>Brain tumors</u><br><br>* <u>Brainstem</u> (<u>pontine</u>) hemorrhage<br><br>* <u>Demyelinating</u> disease (e.g., <u>multiple sclerosis</u>)<br><br>* <u>Malformations</u> (e.g., <u>Arnold-Chiari</u>)<br><br>* <u>Meningitis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Preganglionic</u> | <br>* Ciliospinal center (second-order oculosympathetic neuron) → pulmonary apex → stellate <u>ganglion</u> → <u>superior cervical ganglion</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Tumors (e.g., <u>breast</u> or <u>lung cancer</u> compressing <u>stellate ganglion</u>, esp. <u>Pancoast tumor</u>)<br><br>* <u>Iatrogenic</u> (e.g., <u>birth trauma</u>, <u>central venous catheterization</u>)<br><br>* <u>Lymphadenopathy</u><br><br>* Arterial lesions/dissection: aorta, subclavian, <u>common carotid</u><br><br>* <u>Cervical rib</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Postganglionic</u> | <br>* <u>Superior cervical ganglion</u> (third-order oculosympathetic neuron) → <u>internal carotid artery</u> and ophthalmic nerve → <u>iris dilator muscle</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Dissection of the <u>internal carotid artery</u><br><br>* <u>Cluster headache</u><br><br>* <u>Cavernous sinus</u> [[1]](/library/XtX9X-)<br><br>* <u>Tumor</u><br><br>* <u>Herpes zoster</u> infection<br><br><br> |

---

## Clinical features

* Triad of Horner syndrome  

* <u>Miosis</u> (constriction of the <u>pupil</u>)

* Occurs because the sympathetically controlled <u>iris dilator muscle</u> fails to contract

* Leads to <u>anisocoria</u> and a dilation lag on exam

* Partial <u>ptosis</u> (drooping of the upper <u>eyelid</u>)

* Occurs because the sympathetically controlled <u>superior tarsal muscle</u> fails to keep the upper <u>eyelid</u> raised

* It is milder than <u>ptosis</u> associated with <u>oculomotor nerve</u> or <u>levator palpebrae</u> muscle lesions.

* Anhidrosis (absence of sweating) or reduced sweating on the face and arm, depending on the location of the lesion

* Occurs because the <u>sympathetic</u> innervation of the facial <u>sweat glands</u> is impaired

* Seen in central and <u>preganglionic</u> lesions

* <u>Facial flushing</u> due to vasodilatation

* (Apparent) <u>enophthalmos</u>

* Associated symptoms depending on the etiology:

* <u>Atrophy</u> of arm and hand muscles

* <u>Pain</u> in the neck or face





> [!NOTE]
> Remember the symptoms of Horner syndrome by the great HORNs of the PAMpas deer: Ptosis, Anhidrosis, and Miosis.
